articles.title: Digital Phenotyping, Remote Monitoring, and Risk Prediction of Heart Failure in Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy: A Systematic Review With Narrative Synthesis

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDPs), particularly preeclampsia, are associated with acute cardiovascular morbidity and future heart failure (HF). Current surveillance relies largely on blood pressure, symptoms, laboratory abnormalities, and clinician-triggered evaluation. Digital phenotyping, remote monitoring, electronic health record-based prediction, and machine learning may enable earlier cardiovascular risk identification.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To systematically identify and narratively synthesize studies evaluating remote monitoring, digital health, machine learning, or risk-prediction approaches for HF-related phenotypes or cardiovascular morbidity in HDPs.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched for studies published from January 2020 through April 10, 2025. Studies evaluating prediction or monitoring approaches in HDPs underwent sequential assessment for HF-related or cardiovascular morbidity outcomes. Screening and full-text reviews were performed by 2 independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Given substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Of 3366 records imported for screening, 6 studies met the inclusion criteria. Studies used clinical prediction models, electronic health record (EHR)-based models, and remote monitoring to evaluate acute cardiovascular morbidity, HFpEF, cardiac remodeling, and cardiovascular readmission. Model discrimination ranged from modest to strong (AUROC approximately 0.70-0.94). Recurrent predictors included severe hypertensive disease, earlier gestational age at delivery, kidney disease, pre-existing cardiac disease, pulmonary hypertension, maternal age, obesity-related measures, blood pressure, and postpartum volume retention. Most prediction models lacked external validation.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Preliminary evidence suggests that clinical, EHR-derived, and remotely monitored data may support risk stratification for selected cardiovascular morbidity and HF-related phenotypes after HDPs. Prospective validation, physiological marker integration, and evaluation of risk-guided interventions are needed.

articles.conclusion: Preliminary evidence suggests that clinical, EHR-derived, and remotely monitored data may support risk stratification for selected cardiovascular morbidity and HF-related phenotypes after HDPs. Prospective validation, physiological marker integration, and evaluation of risk-guided interventions are needed.

articles.title: Cardiac Damage and Clinical Outcomes in Symptomatic Severe Aortic Stenosis Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The extent of cardiac damage in patients with aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with worse clinical outcomes.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: This study sought to investigate the clinical impact of cardiac damage using the updated criteria incorporating the echocardiographic probability of pulmonary hypertension.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: This post hoc subanalysis of LANDMARK trial, which randomized 768 patients with severe AS to the Myval transcatheter heart valve (THV) series or to contemporary THVs (Sapien and Evolut series), used updated cardiac damage classification: stage 0, no cardiac damage; stage 1, left ventricular damage; stage 2, left atrial or mitral valve damage; stage 3, pulmonary artery or tricuspid valve damage; and stage 4, right ventricular damage. The impact of cumulative cardiac damage, defined as meeting all criteria for stages 1 to 4, was also assessed. The primary endpoint was 1-year all-cause mortality.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Cardiac damage stages were assessed in 596 patients (stage 0, n = 36; stage 1, n = 88; stage 2, n = 284; stage 3, n = 84; stage 4, n = 104), with a mean age of 80.2 (5.7) years and a mean Society of Thoracic Surgeons score of 3.3% (2.4%). One-year mortality was 0%, 1.1%, 4.7%, 7.2%, and 20.4% in stages 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively (log-rank P < 0.001). The area under the curve for predicting 1-year mortality was 0.739. Patients with cumulative cardiac damage had the highest mortality (23.6%). In the multivariable analysis, stage 4 was independently associated with higher 1-year mortality.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: The updated cardiac damage staging stratified 1-year mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement, highlighting the importance of comprehensive echocardiographic assessment in severe AS. (LANDMARK Trial: a Randomised Controlled Trial of Myval THV [LANDMARK]; NCT04275726).

articles.conclusion: The updated cardiac damage staging stratified 1-year mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement, highlighting the importance of comprehensive echocardiographic assessment in severe AS. (LANDMARK Trial: a Randomised Controlled Trial of Myval THV [LANDMARK]; NCT04275726).

articles.title: Prognostic value of right atrial pressure to cardiac output slope in patients undergoing exercise right heart catheterization
authors: PEX-NET (Pulmonary Haemodynamics during Exercise Network) ERS Clinical Research Collaboration
articles.journal: Annals of the American Thoracic Society

abstract.label: BACKGROUND/AIMS
abstract.text: This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of the right atrial pressure to cardiac output relationship (RAP/CO-slope) from rest to end exercise in patients undergoing exercise right heart catheterization for suspected or confirmed pulmonary hypertension (PH).

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The analysis used data from the retrospective arm of the Pulmonary Hemodynamics during Exercise Network (PEX NET), a multicenter collaboration involving 23 PH centers. Patients were included if resting and exercise measurements were obtained in the same body position and if RAP/CO-slopes were available. Cox proportional hazard models adjusted for age, sex, and hemoglobin were applied. Time dependent ROC curves were used to identify a prognostic cut off.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 856 patients were included (median age 59 years; 67% female), of whom 336 had PH. Over a median follow up of 6.5 years, 114 patients (13%) died. Higher RAP/CO-slopes were independently associated with increased mortality, even after adjusting for established resting and exercise hemodynamics (hazard ratio 1.08, 95%CI: 1.03-1.13, p < 0.001). Among patients with manifest PH at rest, a RAP/CO-slope ≥1.0 mmHg·min·L⁻¹ was linked to a 2.2 fold higher mortality risk (hazard ratio: 2.20; 95% CI: 1.1-4.5; p = 0.032) compared with slopes <1.0 mmHg·min·L⁻¹. In a multivariable model including NT proBNP, 6 minute walking distance, and WHO functional class, the RAP/CO-slope remained the strongest predictor of mortality.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: The RAP/CO-slope is a strong, independent prognostic marker across a spectrum of RV afterload stress. A RAP/CO slope ≥1 mmHg·min·L⁻¹ was identified as particularly predictive in manifest PH.

articles.conclusion: The RAP/CO-slope is a strong, independent prognostic marker across a spectrum of RV afterload stress. A RAP/CO slope ≥1 mmHg·min·L⁻¹ was identified as particularly predictive in manifest PH.

articles.title: Unraveling Severe Myocardial Dysfunction in Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome: Beyond Septic Shock

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Group A Streptococcus is a clinically important yet underrecognized cause of inflammatory myocardial dysfunction, capable of triggering shock through toxin-mediated injury and inflammation.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 19-year-old woman presented with progressive fatigue, severe hypotension, and a purpuric chest rash. Laboratory investigation showed rising troponin, leukocytosis, and lactic acidosis. Echocardiography and right heart catheterization revealed significant biventricular dysfunction. She developed shock requiring mechanical circulatory support with an Impella CP and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin were initiated empirically for presumed inflammatory myocarditis. Chest wall biopsy grew Group A Streptococcus, supporting the diagnosis of streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (STSS). Ultimately, she recovered cardiac function with mechanical circulatory support and targeted antimicrobial therapy.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This case highlights severe, reversible myocardial dysfunction because of STSS.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
abstract.text: STSS can precipitate severe, reversible myocardial dysfunction representing a mixed septic-cardiogenic phenotype that may mimic fulminant myocarditis.

articles.title: Transcatheter Mitral Cerclage Ventriculoplasty: 5-Year Outcomes

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Transcatheter mitral cerclage ventriculoplasty places a circumferential tensioning loop around the base of the left ventricle to reduce mitral annular dimensions and reshape ventricular geometry in patients with functional mitral regurgitation and heart failure. Early experience demonstrated reductions in mitral regurgitation and improvements in heart failure symptoms.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Division of Intramural Research Transcatheter Mitral Cerclage Ventriculoplasty Early Feasibility Study was an investigator-initiated, prospective, multicenter study. Between 1 and 5 years, vital status, serious adverse events, routine clinical documentation, and site-reported transthoracic echocardiography findings were collected.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Nineteen procedures were attempted in 18 participants (63% heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, 37% heart failure with preserved ejection fraction). Median age was 73 years, and 63% were female. Kaplan-Meier estimated 5-year survival was 57%. One participant underwent left ventricular assist device implantation after 2 years, and 1 participant underwent mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair after 3 years; none underwent heart transplantation. The study was suspended after complete heart block developed in 6 participants, including 4 requiring new cardiac implantable electronic devices. Among participants with available follow-up echocardiography, site-reported imaging demonstrated mitral regurgitation reduction and improved left ventricular ejection fraction through 5 years. Symptomatic improvement was most apparent during the first year and attenuated thereafter.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Cerclage ventriculoplasty was associated with mitral regurgitation reduction and improved ventricular function among participants with available long-term follow-up. Symptomatic benefit was greatest during the first year and diminished thereafter, suggesting that favorable remodeling may not fully offset progression of the underlying cardiomyopathy.

abstract.label: REGISTRATION
abstract.text: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT03929913.

articles.conclusion: Cerclage ventriculoplasty was associated with mitral regurgitation reduction and improved ventricular function among participants with available long-term follow-up. Symptomatic benefit was greatest during the first year and diminished thereafter, suggesting that favorable remodeling may not fully offset progression of the underlying cardiomyopathy.

articles.title: Phenotyping of Exercise Response in FORMs of Arrhythmogenic CardioMyopathy: PERFORM-ACM
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Heart and circulatory physiology
articles.journal_abbrev: Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol
articles.ta: Am J Physiol Heart Circ Physiol

abstract.text: Patients with arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM) are advised to perform no more than moderate-intensity exercise, but whether such exercise acutely alters hemodynamic, electrophysiological, or cardiac biomarker profiles is unknown. We investigated whether moderate-intensity isometric, resistance, or aerobic exercise induces exercise pulmonary hypertension (exPH, mean pulmonary artery pressure to cardiac output slope >3 mmHg/L/min), troponin T elevation, or changes in late potentials (LP) in definitive or probable ACM. Twenty patients (13 definitive, 7 probable ACM; age 42.2 ± 10.7 years) underwent exercise right heart catheterization during isometric handgrip (HG) and bicep curl (BC) (1 minute each at 70% of maximal voluntary contraction), followed by 2 × 20 minutes of supine cycling (CYC) at the first ventilatory threshold. Central hemodynamics and cardiac biomarkers were measured during each condition, and high-density right ventricular electroanatomical mapping was performed before and after exercise. exPH did not occur in either group (all <3 mmHg/L/min), whereas troponin T rose progressively without group differences (p=0.880). LP within the "arrhythmogenic triangle" decreased in probable (mean change -1.95 ± 1.59%) but increased in definitive ACM (mean change 2.72 ± 2.16%, p<0.001). In conclusion, moderate-intensity HG, BC, and CYC exercise were not associated with exPH in probable or definitive ACM. Despite similar hemodynamic and biomarker responses, post-exercise LP diverged between groups, decreasing in probable but increasing in definitive ACM. This observation warrants validation in larger cohorts with better control for baseline substrate and longitudinal clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Clinical effects of istaroxime in acute heart failure and cardiogenic shock: A patient-level pooled analysis of four phase II randomized clinical trials

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Istaroxime is an inotropic and lusitropic agent tested in acute heart failure (AHF) or AHF-related cardiogenic shock (AHF-CS). We aimed to assess its efficacy and concy in a pooled analysis of all randomized trials performed to date.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Patient-level data from four phase II randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials were pooled. The effects of istaroxime 0.5-1.0 µg/kg/min for up to 48 hours vs. placebo on hemodynamics, cardiac function, and clinical outcomes were assessed.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 284 patients were included (n=200 AHF, n=84 AHF-CS). Compared with placebo, istaroxime increased systolic blood pressure through 6 hours (least square [LS] mean difference in the area under the change from baseline curve 28.9 mmHg*h, 95% CI 18.1 to 39.8 mmHg*h) and through 24 hours (LS mean difference 121.4 mmHg*h, 95% CI 63.9 to 179.0 mmHg*h). Reductions in heart rate, body weight, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and echocardiographic E/e' ratio, and an increase in echocardiographic stroke work index and stroke volume were observed with istaroxime, with a numerically greater improvement in invasive cardiac output and creatinine. Numerically, dyspnea and quality of life were improved, and length of index hospitalization, worsening HF and death were lower with istaroxime. Serious adverse events were similar between the istaroxime and placebo arms.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In this patient-level pooled analysis, istaroxime 0.5-1.0 µg/kg/min was associated with improvement in SBP and hemodynamic and echocardiographic measurements of cardiac performance, without tachycardia or serious safety concerns. These findings support a phase III program to investigate the impact of istaroxime administration on outcomes.

articles.conclusion: In this patient-level pooled analysis, istaroxime 0.5-1.0 µg/kg/min was associated with improvement in SBP and hemodynamic and echocardiographic measurements of cardiac performance, without tachycardia or serious safety concerns. These findings support a phase III program to investigate the impact of istaroxime administration on outcomes.

articles.title: Hemodynamic effects of semaglutide in individuals with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial

abstract.text: The glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist semaglutide improves symptoms in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) through unclear mechanisms. Here, in this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, we randomly assigned 81 patients (47 women) with HFpEF and obesity to semaglutide (2.4 mg weekly) or placebo for 52 weeks. The primary outcome was the change in invasively measured pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP), a direct measure of cardiac congestion, during low-intensity exercise. Additional mechanistic outcomes included other hemodynamic measures and hemodynamic HFpEF remission (defined as normal PAWP under conditions of both rest and exercise at 52 weeks). At baseline, PAWP was 17.5 ± 4.3 mmHg at rest and 31.7 ± 5.2 mmHg during exercise. After 52 weeks, the mean change in PAWP during exercise was -9.8 (95% confidence interval (CI): -11.3 to -8.2) mmHg with semaglutide and +0.9 (95% CI: -1.3 to 3.0) mmHg with placebo (estimated difference, -10.6 mmHg; 95% CI: -13.3 to -8.0; P < 0.0001). As compared to placebo, semaglutide also decreased resting PAWP (estimated difference, -7.1 mmHg; 95% CI: -9.8 to -4.4; P < 0.0001), and semaglutide-treated patients were more likely to experience hemodynamic remission (53.7% versus 7.4%, odds ratio = 14.1, 95% CI: 3.0-134.6, P < 0.001). The results from this trial indicate that, in patients with HFpEF and obesity, treatment with semaglutide reduced left heart filling pressures during exercise and at rest and was associated with hemodynamic HFpEF remission in over half of treated patients. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05371496 .

articles.title: Effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity: a pre-specified cardiac magnetic resonance substudy of the CAMEO-SEMA trial

abstract.text: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists improve symptoms in patients with obesity and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). We recently demonstrated that semaglutide reduces exertional pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) in obesity-related HFpEF, but potential effects of semaglutide on cardiac structure and function that may underlie these hemodynamic improvements remain unclear. In this prespecified cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) substudy of the randomized CAMEO-SEMA trial, 49 participants (33 semaglutide, 16 placebo, 28 female) underwent CMR at baseline and 52 weeks, within 1 day of invasive exercise hemodynamic assessment. The prespecified primary CMR endpoint was change in left atrial (LA) reservoir strain; other prespecified CMR endpoints included LV filling dynamics, which were assessed by early filling rate indexed to end-diastolic volume (eFR/EDV). Compared with placebo, semaglutide improved LA reservoir strain (+5.7% [95% CI, +0.3 to +9.7]; P=0.037) and eFR/EDV (+0.64 s-1 [95% CI, +0.42 to +1.00]; P<0.0001). Improvements in LA reservoir strain and LV filling dynamics were associated with reductions in exercise PAWP (r=-0.46, P<0.001 and r=-0.65, P<0.0001, respectively). With respect to other prespecified CMR endpoints, semaglutide reduced LV mass, restored more physiologic LV geometry, and improved right ventricular function and biventricular myocardial mechanics. The results of this CMR substudy indicate that in patients with obesity-related HFpEF, semaglutide improves LA function and LV diastolic filling dynamics, identifying improvements in myocardial function that may contribute to semaglutide's improvement of hemodynamics. ClinicalTrials.gov number: NCT05371496.

articles.title: Cardiac Cirrhosis Associated With Valvular Heart Disease and Intracardiac Shunting

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Cardiac cirrhosis results from chronic hepatic congestion secondary to right-sided heart failure, causing sinusoidal injury and progressive fibrosis. Its presentation can mimic primary hepatic cirrhosis, creating diagnostic uncertainty.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 41-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse presented with abdominal distention, dyspnea, and edema, with hepatojugular reflux and a holosystolic apical murmur. B-type natriuretic peptide was elevated with normal liver enzymes. Imaging suggested cirrhosis with ascites, but echocardiography revealed severe mitral regurgitation and a large secundum atrial septal defect with right-sided enlargement. Right heart catheterization confirmed elevated right-sided pressures with left-to-right shunting. Paracentesis showed a low serum-ascites albumin gradient and high protein. She was started on diuretics and referred for valve repair and atrial septal defect closure.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Despite imaging suggesting liver disease, labs, examination, and ascitic fluid analysis directed the diagnosis toward a cardiac etiology. Hepatic dysfunction may reverse after correcting the underlying cardiac cause.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: Consider cardiac causes of ascites even when imaging suggests cirrhosis. Work-up should include labs, echocardiography, ascites analysis, and right heart catheterization.

articles.title: Optimal Approach to Implementing an Echocardiography-based Artificial Intelligence Algorithm for Diagnosing Hemodynamically Confirmed HFpEF in a Referral Population

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Diagnosing heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) in outpatients remains challenging. An AI model (EchoGo HF) that analyzes resting apical 4-chamber echocardiographic clips shows promise, but its diagnostic performance relative to gold-standard exercise hemodynamic testing is unknown. Additionally, the optimal approach to integrating the AI-HFpEF model with clinical risk scores has not been established.

abstract.label: METHODS AND RESULTS
abstract.text: This study included outpatients referred for suspected HFpEF, who underwent exercise hemodynamic testing. HFpEF was defined by elevated filling pressures on exercise right-heart catheterization, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure [PCWP] ≥15 mmHg at rest, ≥25 mmHg during exercise, or PCWP/CO ≥2 mmHg/L/min), or resting/exercise echocardiography (E/e' >14). AI-HFpEF was applied to resting echocardiograms, and diagnostic performance (area under the receiver operating characteristic [AUROC] and F1) was compared with the H₂FPEF score. Associations with disease severity (PCWP, peak exercise oxygen uptake [VO₂peak]) were evaluated using multivariable regression. Additionally, the performance of a combined model (H₂FPEF + AI-HFpEF) was assessed using AUROC. Among 280 patients, 222 (79%) had hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF. AI-HFpEF classified 57% (n = 159/280) as HFpEF, 38% (n = 106/280) as no HFpEF and 5% (15/280) as uncertain. AI-HFpEF-detected HFpEF independently predicted elevated PCWP (OR [95% CI] = 2.48[1.17, 5.22]; P = 0.017), and lower VO₂peak (β = -1.38 [-2.64, -0.13] mL/kg/min; P = 0.031). The AI-HFpEF model had good model discrimination (AUROC = 0.702) with an F1 score of 76.8%, a sensitivity of 67.3% (false-negative rate = 32.7%) and a specificity of 68.5% (false-positive rate = 31.5%). Combining H₂FPEF with AI-HFpEF significantly improved performance to detect hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF vs H₂FPEF score alone (0.724 vs 0.656; DeLong P = 0.021). Incorporating the AI-HFpEF model with H₂FPEF score led to greater improvement in detecting hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF among patients with low/intermediate than those with high H₂FPEF scores (AUROC = 0.746 vs 0.535). A 2-step strategy, combining upfront H₂FPEF score assessment with selective AI-HFpEF assessment in participants with low/intermediate H₂FPEF, identified a larger proportion of patients with hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF (78%) vs H₂FPEF score alone (48%). This strategy resulted in a net reclassification improvement of 15.5% and a relative integrated discrimination improvement of 94%.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: AI-HFpEF is independently associated with markers of disease severity, accurately identifies hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF, and improves diagnostic performance when integrated with H₂FPEF, particularly at low/intermediate scores.

articles.conclusion: AI-HFpEF is independently associated with markers of disease severity, accurately identifies hemodynamically confirmed HFpEF, and improves diagnostic performance when integrated with H₂FPEF, particularly at low/intermediate scores.

articles.title: Long-term trajectories of invasive hemodynamic parameters and clinical outcomes after durable left ventricular assist device implantation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Long-term hemodynamic changes after durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation are not well characterized. Characterizing these trajectories is clinically relevant, as persistent or evolving abnormalities in filling pressures and pulmonary circulation may identify patients at risk for adverse outcomes.

abstract.label: METHOD
abstract.text: We conducted a retrospective single-center study including all patients who underwent durable LVAD implantation at the University Medical Center Groningen (2012 to 2025). We evaluated serial right heart catheterization (RHC) measurements to describe hemodynamic trajectories. Repeated measures, mixed-effect models were used to analyze hemodynamic trajectories up to 60 months of follow-up, including mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP), pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP), right atrial pressure (RAP), and pulmonary artery pulsatility index (PAPi). Trajectories were compared according to survivor status, baseline LVAD strategy, development of late right ventricular failure (RVF), presence of aortic regurgitation (AR), and worsening renal function (WRF).

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 199 patients (176 HeartMate 3; 23 HeartMate II), mean PAP (-10.1 mmHg, 95% CI -13.1 to -7.1) and PCWP (-9.9 mmHg, 95% CI -12.5 to -7.2) decreased significantly within the first 6 months after LVAD implantation, while RAP (0.0 mmHg, 95% CI -0.8 to 0.8) remained unchanged. Cardiac index (+0.6 L/min/m², 95% CI 0.4-0.8) and cardiac output (+1.3 L/min, 95% CI 0.9-1.7) increased significantly over the same interval. Beyond 6 months, trajectories for most hemodynamic parameters remained generally stable. Non-survivors and patients developing late RVF showed consistently higher filling pressures with trajectories largely parallel to those of survivors or those without RVF. Hemodynamic trajectories did not differ by initial LVAD strategy. In contrast, clinically significant aortic regurgitation and WRF were associated with distinct hemodynamic trajectories.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: Hemodynamic parameters after durable LVAD implantation improved early and remained largely stable thereafter. Patients with adverse clinical outcomes showed persistently higher and/or altered hemodynamic profiles. These findings suggest that longitudinal hemodynamic assessment may enable early identification of patients at risk for adverse outcomes.

articles.conclusion: Hemodynamic parameters after durable LVAD implantation improved early and remained largely stable thereafter. Patients with adverse clinical outcomes showed persistently higher and/or altered hemodynamic profiles. These findings suggest that longitudinal hemodynamic assessment may enable early identification of patients at risk for adverse outcomes.

articles.title: Treatment of children and young adults with a Fontan circulation and cardiovascular dysfunction. 2026 Consensus Statement from the European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN), endorsed by AHA, AEPC, EACTS, ISACHD, ISHLT and PICS
articles.journal: The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation

abstract.text: The Fontan operation enables long term survival for many individuals born with single ventricle heart disease, but the resulting circulation imposes a lifelong hemodynamic burden and predisposes to cardiovascular dysfunction and multisystem morbidity. Evidence based guidance for assessment and management of Fontan specific cardiac and vascular dysfunction, however, remains limited. The European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN) convened an international, multidisciplinary executive writing group to review the available literature and develop consensus recommendations addressing cardiovascular dysfunction in children and young adults with a Fontan circulation. Recommendations were graded using established Class of Recommendation and Level of Evidence criteria adapted to the Fontan specific evidence base. The statement addresses cardiovascular assessment, pulmonary vascular disease and use of pulmonary vasodilator therapy, Fontan pathway obstruction, systemic venous and arterial abnormalities and collateral vessels, lymphatic dysfunction and intervention, myocardial dysfunction and heart failure therapy, and thromboembolic risk and antithrombotic therapy. The focus is on phenotype-guided management, hemodynamically informed treatment decisions, and medical, transcatheter, and surgical approaches tailored to Fontan circulation. Seven graded recommendation tables as well as a flowchart for considerations regarding pulmonary vasodilator therapy are provided to support clinical decision making. Fontan-specific evidence remains limited, so many recommendations necessarily represent expert opinion. This EPPVDN consensus statement, therefore, discusses knowledge gaps and priorities for collaborative research to improve outcomes for individuals living with a Fontan circulation.

articles.title: Treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children and young adults. 2026 consensus statement from the European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN), endorsed by AHA, AEPC, EACTS, ESPR, PASCAR, PCS, and PICS
articles.journal: The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation

abstract.text: The European Pediatric Pulmonary Vascular Disease Network (EPPVDN) is a registered, non-profit organization dedicated to advancing innovative diagnostic methods and treatment options for all forms of pediatric pulmonary vascular disease, including pulmonary hypertension (PH) related to congenital heart disease (CHD), PH associated with developmental lung disease (DEVLD-PH), persistent PH of the newborn (PPHN), postcapillary PH in left heart disease (PH-LHD), and associated cardiac dysfunction/heart failure. In the past, the EPPVDN has published consensus statements on the diagnosis and treatment of pediatric PH (2016, 2019), which have been endorsed by multiple societies. The executive writing group conducted comprehensive searches of the PubMed/MEDLINE bibliographic database (2000 to 2025) and engaged in multiple web-based and in-person meetings. Thirteen section task forces discussed and created consented recommendations. Prospective clinical studies, clinical trials, meta-analyses, expert consensus guidelines, and other articles with pediatric data were included in the search, using the terms 'pulmonary hypertension' and related keywords. Classes of recommendation (COR) and levels of evidence (LOE) were assigned based on AHA/ESC definitions, pediatric PH studies, adult studies including a minimum N number of 15 children, or studies involving adults with CHD. Classifications and definitions from the 7th World Symposium on Pulmonary Hypertension (WSPH) in 2024 were incorporated and discussed. We produced 6 graded recommendation tables (COR, LOE) and 3 algorithms for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children, and young adults. A total of 16 main and 17 supplemental display items cover a range of topics, including risk assessment, pharmacological therapy, transcatheter interventions and surgery, recommendations specific to PH subgroups/special populations and clinical settings. Adaptation of management recommendations for middle-to-low-income regions is provided. Together, these up-to-date guidelines provide a comprehensive, detailed, and practical framework for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension in infants, children and young adults, aiming to improve outcomes and quality of life for affected patients.

articles.title: Right Heart Dysfunction in Valvular Heart Disease: Epidemiology, Prognosis, and Management Considerations
articles.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology

abstract.text: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is an important determinant of clinical outcomes across a wide range of cardiovascular pathologies. As the prevalence of valvular heart disease (VHD) increases with the aging population, the intersection between RV function and VHD will become all the more relevant for proper risk assessment, treatment selection, and prognostication. Even though RV dysfunction may not always be attributed to VHD, we aim to give clinicians, researchers, and regulators a deep understanding of how patients with VHD should be evaluated for RV dysfunction and treated when RV dysfunction coexists with VHD. We begin with a discussion of the epidemiology and diagnostic evaluation of RV dysfunction in patients with a variety of VHD subgroups, including right-side (ie, associated with the tricuspid valve) and left-side (ie, associated with the mitral and aortic valves) VHD. Attention is also given in that section to contemporary methods and evolving techniques for identifying and phenotyping different forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD. No single imaging test practically or comprehensively captures all degrees and forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD; therefore, the discussion emphasizes integrating evidence from different imaging modalities and hemodynamic assessments. The second component of the review discusses how RV dysfunction affects therapeutic options, including medical, transcatheter, and surgical therapies for VHD. The focus of the discussion is on the interplay between RV dysfunction in patients with right-side VHD, namely tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Unlike left-side VHD, where RV dysfunction is a marker of overall disease severity but does not necessarily indicate futility or nonresponse to therapy, right-side VHD and TR-associated RV dysfunction identifies a subset of patients where intervention may precipitate even worse RV function. The nuances of these interactions between ventricular and valvular function are the emphasis of this section, and we aim to provide a framework for understanding RV function in the context of these different forms of VHD. Finally, the review concludes with an eye to the future, discussing the ways in which RV dysfunction can be identified and managed with the use of novel techniques. This discussion is increasingly relevant as RV dysfunction and VHD frequently coexist, and accurate identification is critical to matching the right treatment for the right patient.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Heart Failure: From Earlier Disease Detection to Integrated Care Delivery

abstract.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly positioned to improve heart failure (HF) care by predicting risk, enabling earlier disease identification, and supporting more reliable delivery of evidence-based management. Current applications span opportunistic detection for low ejection fraction, HF with preserved ejection fraction, and structural heart disease using tools such as AI-enabled electrocardiography, imaging- and electronic health record‒based risk stratification, clinician-facing decision support, remote medication titration, and wearable monitoring platforms. The strongest evidence suggests that AI is most effective when embedded into active clinical workflows that guide targeted testing, treatment optimization, and longitudinal follow-up, rather than functioning as passive alerts alone. This review examines the emerging landscape of AI-enabled HF care delivery from early detection through chronic management, with emphasis on implementation, workflow integration, and the capacity of these tools to improve diagnostic yield and ultimately scalability.

articles.title: Transbaffle Transcatheter Valve-in-Valve Implantation for Systemic Atrioventricular Bioprosthetic Stenosis in a Patient With Fontan Circulation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: We report the case of a 29-year-old woman with an atrioventricular canal defect with left ventricular hypoplasia and mitral atresia in the setting of situs inversus and dextrocardia, palliated with Fontan circulation.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: At 21 years of age, she underwent systemic atrioventricular valve replacement with a 33-mm Hancock II bioprosthesis (Medtronic). Eight years later, she developed progressive bioprosthetic stenosis: mean transvalvular gradient of 11 mm Hg with restricted leaflet motion. Given prohibitive surgical risk, transcatheter valve-in-valve (ViV) implantation using a 29-mm Sapien 3 (Edwards Lifesciences) prosthesis was performed via transbaffle access. The procedure resulted in immediate hemodynamic improvement with reduction of the mean gradient.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Only a few cases of transbaffle ViV implantation in the systemic atrioventricular position in patients with a Fontan circulation have been reported.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
abstract.text: This case illustrates the feasibility of transbaffle ViV implantation in complex Fontan anatomy and highlights transcatheter therapy as a valuable alternative in high-risk adult congenital heart disease.

articles.title: Effects of Transcatheter Tricuspid Edge-to-Edge Repair on Right Heart Dimension and Function
articles.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) has developed as a treatment option for patients experiencing severe tricuspid regurgitation. T-TEER consistently reduces tricuspid regurgitation, but data on subsequent right heart remodeling remain limited. The aim of this study was to evaluate changes in right heart dimension and function after T-TEER using extended echocardiographic follow-up.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The study was based on the international EuroTR (European Registry of Transcatheter Repair for Tricuspid Regurgitation), including patients undergoing T-TEER between 2016 and 2024 at 18 European centers. Eligible were patients with available baseline and follow-up (≥90 days postprocedure) echocardiographic assessment.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 699 patients (mean age, 78±8 years; 56% women) were included in the analysis. Echocardiographic follow-up was performed at a median of 407 days (interquartile range, 205-801 days). Right heart dimensions significantly decreased: right ventricular (RV) midventricular diameter from 40.2±8.9 to 37.1±8.4 mm (P<0.001) and end-diastolic area from 28.7±9.0 to 26.2±9.6 cm2 (P<0.001). Procedural success was significantly associated with positive RV remodeling (odds ratio, 1.82 [95% CI, 1.07-3.09]). For RV function, a decline of fractional area change from 37.8%±10.2% to 33.3%±10.1% (P<0.001), and tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion from 17.4±4.7 to 16.6±4.7 mm (P<0.001) was observed.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: In the subset of surviving patients with available echocardiographic follow-up, treatment with T-TEER led to favorable long-term changes with reduced RV dimension, associated with procedural success. RV function modestly decreased, likely reflecting normalization after volume unloading.

articles.conclusion: In the subset of surviving patients with available echocardiographic follow-up, treatment with T-TEER led to favorable long-term changes with reduced RV dimension, associated with procedural success. RV function modestly decreased, likely reflecting normalization after volume unloading.

articles.title: Prognostic Value of Right Ventricular-Pulmonary Artery Coupling in Mitral Valve Surgery and Impact of Concomitant Tricuspid Valve Repair
articles.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The prognostic impact of baseline right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling on clinical outcomes following mitral valve surgery with specific consideration of concomitant tricuspid valve repair remains uncertain.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A total of 214 patients who underwent mitral valve surgery and presented with moderate tricuspid regurgitation at the index procedure were included. Patients were classified after baseline right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling (impaired versus normal). The primary study end point was a composite outcome of all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization. Secondary study end points included all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Impaired right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling was observed in 112 patients (52%), while 102 patients (48%) had normal right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling. The rate of concomitant tricuspid valve repair was similar between study groups (50.0% versus 49.0%, P=0.886). Impaired right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling was associated with a higher hazard of the composite outcome (adjusted hazard ratio 2.60, 95% CI 1.32-5.14, P=0.006), heart failure hospitalization (adjusted hazard ratio 3.29, 95% CI 1.27-8.54, P=0.014), and all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 2.25, 95% CI 1.11-4.59, P=0.025) during follow-up. Additionally, concomitant tricuspid valve repair in patients with moderate tricuspid regurgitation was associated with a lower hazard of the composite outcome (adjusted hazard ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.26-0.80, P=0.007).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Impaired right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling is a predictor of adverse outcomes after mitral valve surgery. Concomitant tricuspid valve repair for moderate tricuspid regurgitation seems to be associated with improved outcomes.

articles.conclusion: Impaired right ventricular-pulmonary artery coupling is a predictor of adverse outcomes after mitral valve surgery. Concomitant tricuspid valve repair for moderate tricuspid regurgitation seems to be associated with improved outcomes.

articles.title: Disruptions in U.S. Heart Transplantation: When Innovation Outpaces Evidence
articles.journal: The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation

abstract.text: For nearly four decades, heart transplantation was defined by a stable, predictable paradigm: brain-dead donors, ice-cooler transport, uniform three-drug immunosuppression, and biopsy-based surveillance. Within a few years, that paradigm has been upended. In this perspective, we examine the disruptions now reshaping heart transplantation in the United States. Some are desirable: new preservation platforms and the rapid growth of donation after circulatory death, which now accounts for nearly a quarter of U.S. heart transplants, have expanded the donor pool, and cardiac xenotransplantation has reached clinical testing. Others remain controversial: the 2018 allocation policy has altered listing and support practices, normothermic regional perfusion raises unresolved questions about the determination of death, and inconsistent definitions of ischemic intervals undermine comparisons across DCD studies. Still others are troubling: OPTN restructuring, uneven OPO performance, outsourced procurement, rising costs, and press reports of donors showing signs of life have strained public trust. Underlying all of these is a data gap: national registries capture few DCD procurement and preservation variables, and little about recipients' long-term health beyond survival. Innovation has outpaced our ability to evaluate its consequences. We propose a shared DCD clock built on fixed timestamps, national ethical standards for normothermic regional perfusion, transparency in procurement and its costs, longitudinal outcome reporting, and accountability shared by OPOs and transplant centers. The challenge facing the field is no longer simply how to transplant more hearts, but how to ensure that more transplantation becomes better transplantation.

articles.title: Net Prolongation of Life with Ventricular Assist Device Support in Teenagers: Are We There Yet?
articles.journal: The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation

abstract.text: Heart transplantation prolongs survival in children with end-stage heart disease, yet a single donor heart does not provide a normal lifespan. Contemporary graft survival for teenagers is approximately 15 years, the shortest of any pediatric age group, and re-transplantation remains uncommon. For most patients, the first allograft is the only allograft. Recent adult data demonstrating survival with durable mechanical circulatory support comparable to transplantation raise an important question for adolescents: could intentionally extending ventricular assist device (VAD) support through the teenage years, with transplantation deferred to adulthood, increase total life-years? This perspective examines that hypothesis for adolescents with dilated cardiomyopathy. We review the heightened risks of rejection, graft loss, and treatment nonadherence during adolescence; contemporary outcomes with dischargeable durable VADs in children; the potential for myocardial recovery during extended support; and organ allocation policies that may unintentionally discourage a prolonged-support strategy. We also examine patient and family perspectives and discuss unresolved questions regarding stroke risk, allosensitization, long-term quality of life, and optimal timing of transplantation. No prospective data currently support intentional long-term VAD support as a bridge to transplantation in teenagers, and this concept should be viewed as a hypothesis rather than a practice recommendation. However, for carefully selected adolescents who are clinically stable on durable VAD support, delayed transplantation may be a reasonable topic for shared decision-making discussions while acknowledging the substantial uncertainties that remain. As durable device technology continues to improve, evaluating whether prolonged VAD support can achieve net prolongation of life in teenagers warrants prospective investigation.

articles.title: Measured Left Ventricular Mass Ratio for Size-Matching Identifies Graft Failure Risk in Obese Heart Transplantation
articles.journal: The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Optimal donor-recipient size-matching in heart transplantation with obese donors and/or recipients remains uncertain. We sought to validate the measured left ventricular mass (mLVM) ratio using local donor hospital echocardiograms, determine whether obesity modifies the association with 1-year graft failure compared to the predicted heart mass (PHM), and assess the clinical implications of discordance.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: The Donor Heart Study prospectively collected echocardiograms from donation-after-brain-death donors. The associations of local mLVM ratio (donor measured LVM/recipient predicted LVM) and PHM ratio with 1-year graft failure (death or retransplantation) were assessed by adjusted Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic splines with obesity interaction terms.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Among 2,036 heart transplants, size-matching ratios differed significantly by metric within and across obesity groups (all p<0.001). Obesity significantly modified the association between mLVM ratio and 1-year graft failure (interaction: p=0.009), but not PHM ratio. In obese transplants, the mLVM ratio demonstrated a U-shaped (nonlinear interaction: p=0.011) association with 1-year graft failure, with significant adjusted risk at low and high mLVM ratios; where the mLVM ratio captured a unique phenotype associated with graft failure when oversized (>1.20, aHR: 2.50 [95% CI: 1.30-4.82]). Reclassification from PHM to mLVM ratio improved risk classification by 10.4% and concordantly abnormal PHM and mLVM ratios more than doubled the risk of graft failure (aHR: 2.15 [95% CI: 1.10-4.22]) in obese transplantation.

abstract.label: CONCLUSION
abstract.text: In obese transplants, locally derived mLVM ratio may identify high-risk donor-recipient mismatches not captured by the PHM ratio, with increased graft failure risk at both low and high mLVM ratios.

articles.conclusion: In obese transplants, locally derived mLVM ratio may identify high-risk donor-recipient mismatches not captured by the PHM ratio, with increased graft failure risk at both low and high mLVM ratios.

articles.title: Transinnominate Microaxial Flow Pump Placement in a Patient With Failing Fontan Circulation as Bridge to Transplantation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The Impella 5.5 is a temporary microaxial ventricular assist device indicated to unload the left ventricle and support refractory heart failure. Small peripheral arteries and atypical right ventricular anatomy may preclude its use in patients with Fontan circulation.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: We report a 23-year-old man with hypoplastic left heart syndrome palliated to Fontan with refractory heart failure. Impella 5.5 was placed via the innominate artery, providing 4.5 L/min support for 13 days until heart transplantation; he was discharged in good condition.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Transinnominate approach enables effective bridge to transplantation despite small peripheral vessels.

abstract.label: NOVELTY
abstract.text: This is the first reported case of Impella 5.5 as a bridge to transplant placed via transinnominate artery in an adult with failing Fontan circulation and a systemic right ventricle.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
abstract.text: Impella 5.5 via transinnominate access is feasible in select patients with Fontan circulation and small peripheral vessels and serves as an effective bridge to transplantation.

articles.title: Antegrade Dissection and Re-Entry for Recanalization of Traumatic Coronary Artery Dissection

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Traumatic coronary artery dissection (TCAD) is a rare catastrophic complication of blunt chest trauma, often masked by concomitant injuries, posing diagnostic and therapeutic challenges.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 20-year-old man with polytrauma after a motorcycle accident developed cardiogenic shock. Coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) suggested occlusive left anterior descending dissection, confirmed by delayed angiography under extracorporeal membrane oxygenation support. Stingray-based antegrade dissection and re-entry (ADR) with cutting balloon fenestration and drug-coated balloon angioplasty achieved TIMI flow grade 3. Three-month follow-up showed favorable left anterior descending healing and improved cardiac function.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: CCTA enables early TCAD diagnosis. ADR facilitates guidewire passage, and a stentless strategy is preferable in young polytrauma patients at high bleeding risk.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: Maintain suspicion for TCAD after blunt chest trauma, especially with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction features. CCTA aids early diagnosis; ADR-based percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-coated balloon is safe and effective.

articles.title: Risk Stratification and Outcomes of Right Atrial Phasic Function in Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy: A Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Study
articles.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Advanced arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is associated with a high risk of malignant ventricular arrhythmias (MVA) and end-stage heart failure (HF). However, the prognostic role of right atrial (RA) mechanics, as quantified by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR), remains largely unexplored.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Consecutive patients with arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy undergoing CMR between 2014 and 2021 were retrospectively included. Demographics, clinical history, and strain parameters were collected. The primary clinical end points were end-stage HF and MVA.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: A total of 316 patients (mean age 38±15 years; 66.1% men) were included. Over a median follow-up of 5.3 years, 49 developed end-stage HF and 103 experienced MVA outcomes. Multivariable Cox and Fine-Gray models showed that impaired RA reservoir strain was an independent predictor of end-stage HF (hazard ratio [HR] 0.92, 95% CI 0.89-0.96, P<0.001) and MVA outcomes (subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) 0.98, 95% CI 0.96-0.99, P=0.025), with added prognostic value beyond clinical and imaging variables, improving the C-statistic to 0.84 and 0.70, respectively. Kaplan-Meier survival curves indicated that RA reservoir strain <18.6% was associated with higher end-stage HF risk, consistent across subgroups regardless of left ventricular involvement (both log-rank P<0.05). The association between RA reservoir strain <23.0% and MVA was significant in the overall cohort (P<0.001) and in patients without left ventricular involvement (P=0.002), but not in those with left ventricular involvement (P=0.08).

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Lower cardiac magnetic resonance-derived RA reservoir strain was independently associated with end-stage HF and MVA in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and provided incremental prognostic value beyond conventional risk markers. These findings support RA mechanics as a potential complementary component of multichamber CMR risk assessment, pending external validation.

articles.conclusion: Lower cardiac magnetic resonance-derived RA reservoir strain was independently associated with end-stage HF and MVA in arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy and provided incremental prognostic value beyond conventional risk markers. These findings support RA mechanics as a potential complementary component of multichamber CMR risk assessment, pending external validation.

articles.title: Serologic Guidance for Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Selection and Survival Using the Cosmos Dataset
articles.journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)

abstract.text: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a life-support therapy for patients with severe cardiac or respiratory failure. Despite its growing use, evidence-based guidelines for ECMO candidacy remain limited due to small, single-center studies and heterogeneous designs. This study leveraged Epic Cosmos, an electronic health record dataset encompassing over 300 million patient records, to analyze outcomes among 42,210 adults treated with ECMO between January 1, 2019, and February 15, 2026, involving 23,116 (54.8%) venoarterial (VA), 14,632 (34.7%) venovenous (VV), and 4,462 (10.6%) hybrid (VA and VV) cases. Hospital mortality varied from 37% (VV) to 50% (VA). Poisson models by ECMO type for in-hospital mortality adjusted for key demographic and clinical variables showed the admitting diagnosis group had the strongest association with subsequent mortality. Several blood chemistry markers measured within the 24 hours before ECMO initiation were also associated with increased mortality, including elevated lactate, elevated creatinine, and lower pH, though strength of association varied by ECMO type. Our findings support the use of large electronic health record (EHR) datasets for ECMO outcomes research and identify exploratory associations between preinitiation biomarkers and in-hospital mortality that require further validation.

articles.title: A Successful Fontan Completion for Asplenia Syndrome Complicated by a Hiatal Hernia

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Hiatal hernia (HH) in patients with a functional single ventricle can increase pulmonary vascular resistance through lung compression and recurrent aspiration.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A female infant with asplenia, functional single ventricle, and HH presented with lung compression. We prioritized HH repair and gastrostomy placement at 8 months of age, successfully alleviating compression and preventing aspiration. She subsequently underwent a bilateral bidirectional Glenn procedure at 1 year and an extracardiac Fontan procedure at 2 years, demonstrating excellent postoperative hemodynamics.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Prioritizing HH repair in patients with single ventricle optimizes pulmonary compliance, providing a safe bridge to Fontan completion when hemodynamically tolerated.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
abstract.text: Early surgical intervention for HH optimizes pulmonary hemodynamics, safely bridging patients with single ventricle to Fontan completion.

articles.title: Catheter-Based Selective Pulmonary Artery Digital Subtraction Angiography and Microvascular Reserve Quantification in Fontan Patient

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Fontan circulation allows univentricular congenital heart physiology to survive. Pulmonary microvascular images are poorly described in live patients during follow-up.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 25-year-old man with a diagnosis of tricuspid atresia status after extracardiac fenestrated Fontan surgery performed at 3 years of age, followed by fenestration device closure a year later, and with a history of hemoptysis at 9 years of age. Follow-up was performed through cardiac catheterization with selective pulmonary artery (PA) digital subtraction angiography (DSA). A decreased percentage of microvascular reserve associated with increased D-dimer suggested in situ thrombosis, and thromboprophylaxis was switched from aspirin to direct oral anticoagulation.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: We focus on catheter-based PA DSA microvascular reserve percentage, cardiopulmonary exercise test, and D-dimer quantification to generate evidence of in situ microvascular thrombosis.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
abstract.text: Catheter-based PA DSA revealing reduced microvascular reserve may identify in situ microvascular thrombosis and offer a novel pathophysiological insight in patients with Fontan circulation during follow-up.

articles.title: Staged Transcatheter Valve-in-Valve Replacement for Simultaneous Failure of 3 Surgical Bioprosthetic Valves

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: To describe a heart team-driven staged transcatheter strategy for accelerated triple bioprosthetic valve failure in a patient with prohibitive surgical risk.

abstract.label: KEY STEPS
abstract.text: A 78-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus, stage 4 chronic kidney disease, permanent atrial fibrillation, and severe frailty presented with NYHA functional class III heart failure. She had undergone triple surgical bioprosthetic heart valve replacement 8 years earlier. Imaging demonstrated severe aortic, mitral, and tricuspid bioprosthetic valve failure. Given prohibitive surgical risk, a staged transcatheter strategy was selected. Valve-in-valve transcatheter aortic valve replacement with a 23-mm supra-annular self-expanding valve and bioprosthetic valve fracture was performed first, followed by valve-in-valve (ViV)-transcatheter mitral valve replacement and ViV transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement with 26-mm balloon-expandable valves. All procedures were successful without complications. At 2 months, NYHA functional class improved from III to II, with satisfactory function of all 3 valves.

abstract.label: POTENTIAL PITFALLS
abstract.text: Coronary obstruction, patient-prosthesis mismatch, neo-left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and hemodynamic intolerance.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: Staged triple ViV intervention may provide a feasible alternative to redo surgery. Multimodality imaging and individualized sequencing are critical.

articles.title: Peritoneal Dialysis for Refractory Ascites in Fontan-Associated Liver Disease

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Fontan-associated liver disease and refractory ascites represent advanced systemic failure in patients with Fontan circulation, with limited therapeutic options.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 38-year-old woman with tricuspid atresia, after a Fontan procedure, developed progressive Fontan-associated liver disease and recurrent refractory ascites. Imaging showed portal hypertension and cirrhosis, and liver biopsy confirmed advanced congestive hepatopathy with stage V fibrosis. She was not a candidate for transplant or further intervention, so a tunneled peritoneal catheter was placed for palliative drainage.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Refractory ascites reflects Fontan failure and a worse prognosis. Conventional therapy is insufficient, and diuretic resistance becomes common. Peritoneal dialysis allows gradual decongestion with reduced hemodynamic stress in preload-dependent circulation. Evidence supports decreased hospital admissions in refractory heart failure, although data in Fontan cases remain limited.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: Refractory ascites is a marker for end-stage Fontan failure. Peritoneal ultrafiltration becomes a palliative choice when definitive therapies are not feasible.

articles.title: Cardiac CT in a Criss-Cross Heart With Double-Outlet Right Ventricle Guiding Single-Ventricle Palliation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Criss-cross heart with double-outlet right ventricle (DORV) and dual discordance is a rare phenotype challenging the conventional echocardiographic segmental characterization.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: An infant with prenatally diagnosed complex congenital heart disease had functionally univentricular physiology, severe pulmonary stenosis, and large septal defects. Echocardiography suggested double-inlet left ventricle with transposed great arteries but incompletely defined segmental anatomy and pulmonary arteries. Electrocardiographically gated cardiac computed tomography (CT) angiography established criss-cross atrioventricular relationships with clockwise ventricular rotation, straddling tricuspid valve, DORV from a mildly hypoplastic morphologic right ventricle, severe subpulmonary/pulmonary annular obstruction, confluent pulmonary arteries, single coronary artery pattern, and patent ductus arteriosus, supporting staged single-ventricle palliation.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: CT provided the segmental and vascular roadmap for staged palliation.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: Criss-cross heart with DORV and dual discordance frequently precludes biventricular repair, directing single-ventricle planning. CT is pivotal pre and postoperatively, defining pulmonary artery eligibility for cavopulmonary connection and confirming the substrate for Fontan completion.

articles.title: Hemodynamic Challenges After Paraganglioma Resection in Fontan-Palliated Adult With Fontan-Associated Liver Disease

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Chronic hypoxemia in cyanotic congenital heart disease is associated with increased risk of pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (PPGL), particularly among patients with single-ventricle physiology.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 26-year-old man with unbalanced atrioventricular septal defect and extracardiac Fontan palliation, and Fontan-associated liver disease presented with hypertensive crisis, with imaging evidence of PPGL. The patient underwent robotic right adrenalectomy and nodule resection complicated by high-volume chylous ascites for several weeks.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Chronic hypoxemia in cyanotic congenital heart disease, particularly univentricular physiology, is a well-established driver of PPGL. Existing guidelines mandate preoperative α-blockade and volume expansion for functional PPGL, but this approach is not tailored to Fontan physiology.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: We present a rare case of operative disruption of retroperitoneal lymphatics superimposed on Fontan-associated systemic venous and lymphatic congestion. Right heart catheterization, cautious α-blockade with volume expansion, and multidisciplinary perioperative management are essential to balance catecholamine blockade against the risks of venous congestion, lymphatic failure, bleeding, and thrombosis.

articles.title: Recalibration of Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring Devices on Serial Catheterization in Adults With Fontan Circulation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: There are limited data on long-term accuracy of invasive hemodynamic monitoring (IHM) in patients with nonpulsatile Fontan circulation (FC).

abstract.label: FIRST-IN-HUMAN/EARLY REPORTS SUMMARY
abstract.text: In a retrospective review of 20 patients with FC and CardioMEMS IHM implanted (2015-2025), simultaneous IHM and invasive mean pulmonary artery pressure measurements were available during 6 repeat catheterizations in 6 patients. IHM readings were nearly all lower than invasive measurements, with the absolute difference ranging from 1 to 10 mm Hg.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION/NOVELTY
abstract.text: There are limited reports of recalibration data with IHM, and to our knowledge this is the first report of simultaneous IHM and invasive measurement in adults with FC. IHM accuracy is important with FC as small pressure differences can greatly affect physiology.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: IHM can provide outpatient pulmonary artery pressure measurements in patients with FC. Because we find discrepancy in device measurements in our cohort, we recommend recalibration with each hemodynamic catheterization in this population.

articles.title: Kidney Transplantation in an Adult With a Fontan Circulation: Targeting Renal Perfusion Pressure

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Dialysis is poorly tolerated in Fontan circulation because of preload-dependent maintenance of cardiac output in the face of passive pulmonary circulation. Evidence that Fontan cardiac output can support kidney-only transplantation remains limited.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 24-year-old woman with situs inversus, congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries, pulmonary atresia, and ventricular septal defect palliated with a fenestrated lateral tunnel Fontan developed stage 5 chronic kidney disease from immune-complex glomerulonephritis. Multidisciplinary evaluation supported preemptive kidney-only transplantation based on preserved ventricular function and stable mixed venous oxygen saturation (60%-63%). She remained dialysis-free with excellent 6-month allograft function (creatinine 1.03 mg/dL).

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: Perioperative management targeting renal perfusion pressure (mean arterial pressure minus central venous pressure ≥55-60 mm Hg), maintaining near-baseline Fontan pressures, and using mixed venous oxygen saturation-guided assessment supported immediate graft function.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: In carefully selected patients with Fontan circulation without evidence of Fontan failure, optimization guided by mean arterial pressure minus central venous pressure may enable kidney-only transplantation, avoiding higher-risk heart-kidney transplantation.

articles.title: VA-ECMO Bridge to Transplant in Acute Fontan Circulatory Failure: A Transpulmonary Gradient-Guided Approach to Weaning

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Little is known about strategies for managing adults with Fontan circulation who require temporary mechanical circulatory support.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 33-year-old woman with Fontan circulation presented with syncope and was found to have Fontan conduit stenosis with low cardiac output. The patient developed hemodynamic collapse during catheter-based intervention, necessitating veno-arterial extracorporeal circulatory membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) cannulation. She was supported by VA-ECMO and was successfully bridged to heart transplantation after 11 days of support.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: In a patient with acute Fontan circulatory failure, temporary mechanical support with VA-ECMO and a Fontan-tailored approach to ramp trial and weaning studies ultimately led to informed clinical decision-making and bridge to successful heart transplant.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGES
abstract.text: VA-ECMO can be used for temporary mechanical circulatory support in acute Fontan failure. Patients with Fontan circulation on VA-ECMO require careful management, with a thoughtful approach to hemodynamics given the circuit's unique physiology.

articles.title: Incidental Hepatocellular Carcinoma on Explant Pathology in Patients With Fontan Circulation After Heart-Liver Transplantation

abstract.text: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is an increasingly recognized complication of Fontan-associated liver disease (FALD), yet diagnosis remains challenging. We describe 4 patients with Fontan circulation in whom HCC was identified incidentally on explant pathology following combined heart-liver transplantation (CHLT). All patients underwent transplantation for Fontan circulatory failure and had hepatic lesions identified on surveillance imaging that were indeterminate for HCC with normal alpha-fetoprotein levels. Explant pathology revealed well- or moderately differentiated HCC in all cases. Among the 3 patients who survived transplantation, none have experienced recurrence to date. These cases highlight the limitations of current surveillance strategies in a subset of patients with FALD referred for CHLT. Further studies are needed to develop imaging criteria and biomarkers specifically validated for FALD-HCC.

articles.title: Emergency Percutaneous Thromboembolectomy in an Adult With Fontan Circulation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Thromboembolic complications remain a major source of morbidity in patients with Fontan circulation, particularly in older atriopulmonary connections with atrial arrhythmias.

abstract.label: CASE SUMMARY
abstract.text: A 54-year-old man with tricuspid atresia and Fontan circulation presented with acute hypoxemia and chest pain after diagnosis of a large right atrial thrombus. Imaging confirmed embolization into the pulmonary artery. Considering a future heart transplantation strategy, the multidisciplinary team opted for percutaneous thrombectomy rather than surgery. The procedure resulted in rapid clinical improvement without complications.

abstract.label: DISCUSSION
abstract.text: This case highlights the complexity of thromboembolism management in Fontan patients and illustrates the feasibility of percutaneous thrombectomy as a bridge-to-transplant strategy in selected patients.

abstract.label: TAKE-HOME MESSAGE
abstract.text: Percutaneous thrombectomy may represent an effective option for acute pulmonary embolism in selected Fontan patients.

articles.title: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Psychometric Validation of the Traditional Chinese emPHasis-10 in Taiwanese Patients With Pulmonary Hypertension

abstract.text: The emPHasis-10 is a brief, disease-specific patient-reported outcome measure for assessing health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in pulmonary hypertension (PH), but a Taiwanese Traditional Chinese version has not been validated. This study translated and culturally adapted the emPHasis-10 into Taiwanese Traditional Chinese (emPHasis-10-T) and evaluated its psychometric properties in patients with PH. A total of 103 clinically stable outpatients with cardiologist-confirmed PH and World Health Organization functional class I-III were recruited from a tertiary medical center in northern Taiwan. Translation and cross-cultural adaptation followed the six-stage Beaton protocol, and psychometric evaluation included confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and associations with external measures. The published three-factor higher-order model improved upon the original one-factor model (CFI = 0.965 vs. 0.930), although an improper parameter estimate was observed. A post hoc modified one-factor model demonstrated the most favorable fit (CFI = 0.988, TLI = 0.983, RMSEA = 0.051, SRMR = 0.030), with standardized loadings of 0.662-0.882. Internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.934) and composite reliability (0.934) were high, and average variance extracted was 0.588. Test-retest reliability yielded an ICC of 0.92 (95% CI: [0.45, 0.98]), although the wide confidence interval indicated limited precision. Convergent validity was supported by a strong correlation with the MLHFQ-PH (r = 0.914), and significant associations were also observed with the EQ-5D Index, HADS-Anxiety, HADS-Depression, and 6-min walk distance (all p < 0.001). The emPHasis-10-T shows promising psychometric properties for PH-specific HRQoL assessment in Taiwan, although its factor structure and temporal stability require further confirmation.

articles.title: Hyperreactivity of Pulmonary Vasculature in Children With Pulmonary Hypertension at Altitude and the Importance of the Prolonged Hyperoxia Test (O2Test)

abstract.text: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is defined hemodynamically, but pulmonary vascular reversibility may provide additional prognostic information, particularly in children exposed to chronic hypobaric hypoxia. We retrospectively analyzed 85 patients diagnosed with PH during childhood at high altitude in Bogotá, Colombia (2,640 m). Seventy-seven underwent cardiac catheterization and 78 underwent a prolonged hyperoxia test (O2Test), consisting of supplemental oxygen at FiO2 > 0.80 for 4-24 h with echocardiographic assessment of pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP). A > 20% reduction in baseline PASP was considered a positive response. Seventy-two patients (84.7%) had severe PH. Among the 78 patients undergoing O2Testing, 49 (62.8%) had a positive response. Patients with a positive O2Test were younger at diagnosis than nonresponders (median, 2 vs. 7 years; p = 0.0061), had lower mean pulmonary artery pressure (55 vs. 83 mmHg; p = 0.0047), and were more frequently in World Health Organization functional class I-II. A negative O2Test was substantially more frequent among patients who died than among survivors (74.1% vs. 17.6%; p < 0.001). Patients with the longest follow-up were predominantly diagnosed before 3 years of age and demonstrated preserved pulmonary vascular reactivity. These findings suggest that pulmonary vascular reactivity to prolonged hyperoxia is associated with age at diagnosis, hemodynamic severity, functional status, and long-term outcome in children with PH living at high altitude. The O2Test may provide complementary information to conventional acute vasoreactivity testing in this population.

articles.title: Harnessing Lung-Kidney Crosstalk: A Novel Ex Vivo Platform for Donor Lung Rehabilitation
articles.journal: The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: The lack of perfusate metabolic homeostasis during ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) may impair lung physiology or stability and limit the application of advanced donor lung therapies. There is evidence that additional organ support during EVLP can improve graft preservation and transplant outcomes. We hypothesized that incorporation of a kidney into an EVLP circuit would maintain perfusate homeostasis and improve lung preservation and metabolic activity.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: A novel circuit was developed to allow simultaneous normothermic perfusion of lungs and kidney in parallel. Donor pig lungs underwent 12 hours of cellular EVLP (EVLP, n=5) or combined cellular ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion (EVLKP, n=5). Lung function was assessed hourly and inflammatory cytokines, edema formation, hemolysis, histologic injury, and kidney performance were evaluated.

abstract.label: RESULTS
abstract.text: Simultaneous lung and kidney perfusion achieved target pulmonary and renal perfusion parameters with stable hemodynamics. EVLKP demonstrated trends of higher compliance, lower inspiratory pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance. Perfusate lactate concentration in EVLKP was markedly lower (P<0.0001), glucose concentrations were higher (P=0.0102), and pH shifted towards physiologic levels (P=0.0009) compared to EVLP. Oxygenation capacity was comparable between groups. Kidney perfusion remained stable throughout EVLKP.

abstract.label: CONCLUSIONS
abstract.text: Combined ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion is safe and feasible in a large-animal model for prolonged lung perfusion. EVLKP improved perfusate homeostasis compared with EVLP alone, which is associated with trends of improvement in lung physiologic parameters. These findings suggest that kidney-derived metabolic and biological support may provide benefits beyond perfusate filtration and highlight the potential importance of organ-organ crosstalk during ex vivo perfusion.

articles.conclusion: Combined ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion is safe and feasible in a large-animal model for prolonged lung perfusion. EVLKP improved perfusate homeostasis compared with EVLP alone, which is associated with trends of improvement in lung physiologic parameters. These findings suggest that kidney-derived metabolic and biological support may provide benefits beyond perfusate filtration and highlight the potential importance of organ-organ crosstalk during ex vivo perfusion.

articles.title: Systemic Microvascular Endothelial Dysfunction in Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction and Type 2 Diabetes: A Pooled Analysis of GLADIATOR-HFpEF, IRON-HFpEF, EMPA-MVD, Hoorn Diabetes Care System, and Healthy Controls

abstract.label: BACKGROUND
abstract.text: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is increasingly recognized as a systemic disorder featuring microvascular dysfunction and metabolic comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the extent to which systemic microvascular abnormalities reflect HFpEF or coexisting T2D remains incompletely understood.

abstract.label: OBJECTIVES
abstract.text: The aim of this study was to characterize systemic microvascular dysfunction in patients with HFpEF and to evaluate the contribution of comorbid T2D.

abstract.label: METHODS
abstract.text: Systemic microvascular function, defined as flow responses expressed as cutaneous vascular conductance, was assessed using laser speckle contrast analysis with iontophoresis of acetylcholine, insulin, and sodium nitroprusside. Analysis adjusted for age and sex were performed across healthy controls (n = 23), T2D (n = 138), HFpEF without T2D (n = 63), and HFpEF with T2D (n = 27).
